masthead.kicker: Hidden Champions of India / a DeepThought series

headline.text: Dynamic Engineers: a 91-year-old founder still on the factory floor, and two years of growth most 67-year-old companies never see again.

subhead.text: A Kolkata fan-and-fan-parts manufacturer whose own founder engineered its production machinery decades ago — now posting back-to-back years of 48% and 94% revenue growth, with two live ISO certifications and one that quietly lapsed.

snapshot.label: Founder
snapshot.value: Sushil Chand Soni, 91, still active daily

p1_engine.eyebrow: A 67-year-old company posting the growth numbers of a startup

blocks.text: **Dynamic Engineers Pvt Ltd** (CIN U29303WB1958PTC024029) was incorporated **18 November 1958** in Kolkata, and is still run by the founding **Soni family** — current directors Pramod Chand Soni, Sukaushal Soni, and Sudarshan Soni. Its founder, **Mr. Sushil Chand Soni, is now 91 and still walks the factory floor almost every day**, per the company's own account: he personally designed the coil-winding and forming machines the business runs on — the production equipment itself was engineered in-house by its founder, not bought off the shelf. That's a specific, hard-to-replicate, tacit-knowledge asset that predates and outlasts any registry certification.
blocks.source: Tofler; ZaubaCorp; company's own LinkedIn post

blocks.text: **The real story here is two consecutive years of fast, genuine growth** — unusual for a 67-year-old manufacturer. Tofler shows revenue in the ₹50-75 crore band for FY24, up **48.18%** year-on-year, with EBITDA up 26.28% and net profit up 38.81%. Tracxn shows FY25 revenue moving into the ₹100-500 crore band, a **94% one-year revenue CAGR**, with EBITDA CAGR of 54%. No public source explains what's driving it — a new large client win, added capacity, or a category tailwind are all plausible, but this is a first-party question worth asking directly. Oddly, paid-up capital has stayed at just **₹10 lakh** throughout — unchanged despite the company now operating at ₹100-500 crore revenue scale, consistent with a family business that has never needed to raise capital by issuing new shares.

The business manufactures **portable fans (pedestal, table, wall, all-metal) and fan parts/accessories**, and the client logos on its own site — **Reliance Industries and Polycab** — point toward a likely component/OEM-supply relationship with larger electrical majors rather than a pure retail-consumer fan brand. Neither relationship was independently corroborated in a direct search, though the site itself reads as a credible, established manufacturer's site rather than a marketing veneer.

The company holds three certifications from recognized bodies: **ISO 14001:2015** for environmental management and **ISO 45001:2018** for occupational health and safety, both current through **March 2027**. Its quality-management certification, **ISO 9001, lapsed in 2024** and hasn't yet been renewed. Industry recognition extends beyond registries too — the company won an **"Innovation and Process Improvement Award" at IFMA's AM Competition 2024 in Delhi**, presented by the Indian Fan Manufacturers Association, a real and active trade body for the sector.

p2_market.eyebrow: A fast-growing market where most of the volume still isn't branded — and Dynamic Engineers sits below the household names

insights.point: India's electric fan market is **large and growing quickly.**
insights.evidence: $1.94 billion (2024) heading to $3.72 billion by 2030, an 11% CAGR — with a separate projection putting the broader market above ₹16,000 crore by 2027-28.

insights.point: But **most of that market still isn't branded at all.**
insights.evidence: The organized/branded segment is only an estimated ~20% share (~₹8,500 crore) of the market, per Havells' own investor materials, with the unorganized segment contributing over ₹1,500 crore in the current fiscal year alone — real headroom for formalization, and a segment where a long-established, certified manufacturer like Dynamic Engineers can credibly compete without needing Havells-level brand marketing.

insights.point: The branded segment itself is a **short list of large, national names** — a different tier from Dynamic Engineers.
insights.evidence: Crompton Greaves, Havells, Orient Electric, Usha International, Bajaj Electricals, Khaitan Electricals, Surya Roshni, Almonard, and Luminous dominate branded retail. Polycab is the most plausible type of counterparty for an OEM/component relationship, since it both brands its own fans and sources components.

insights.point: Industry standing has a real, checkable venue — **IFMA.**
insights.evidence: The Indian Fan Manufacturers Association runs recognized competitions (like the AM Competition referenced above) — a legitimate, if not yet independently confirmed for this company, channel for industry credibility distinct from a government registry.

reflect.text: Dynamic Engineers isn't trying to out-brand Havells or Crompton, and its numbers don't suggest it needs to — it sits underneath the household names, in the much larger unorganized-adjacent and OEM-component layer of the market, riding the same ~11% growth tailwind from a position that doesn't require consumer brand spend. Its real edge is a 67-year operating history, founder-engineered production equipment, and — right now — two years of growth that would be a headline story at a much younger company.

p3_opportunities.lede: Four places worth a closer look, each built on something Dynamic Engineers already has or a gap already visible in its own record.

items.title: Renew ISO 9001
items.body: With two of three certifications already current, letting the quality-management standard lapse is a concrete, fixable gap — arguably the single easiest credibility win available here, especially for any OEM client evaluating the company against fully-certified competitors.

items.title: Turn client logos into referenceable proof
items.body: Reliance Industries and Polycab appear as logos, not case studies. Converting even one of these into a named, specific account of what's supplied and at what scale would do for credibility what the ECL case study did in a comparable profile — real proof beats a bare logo.

items.title: Capture the founder's knowledge before it's lost
items.body: A 91-year-old founder who personally engineered the company's core production machinery is an extraordinary asset and a real succession risk in the same breath. Formal documentation or a structured knowledge-transfer process protects decades of tacit expertise that currently exists mostly in one person's head.

items.title: Formalize and publicize the IFMA standing
items.body: The AM Competition 2024 award is specific and real-sounding, but currently lives only as unverifiable site copy. Confirming and publishing IFMA membership status, and getting the award independently listed or referenced by IFMA itself, would convert a self-claimed credential into a third-party-checkable one.

guesslabel.text: Possibilities, not prescriptions. Which would work, and how much, only Dynamic Engineers' own data and people can tell. Each is small, made to learn fast.

items.title: Get a firm ISO 9001 renewal timeline in writing
items.body: Confirm with the certifying body whether renewal is already underway, and set a target date — a small administrative push that closes the one visible certification gap.

items.title: Request a short reference or case study from one named client
items.body: Ask Reliance Industries or Polycab (whichever relationship is more current/active) for a brief, quotable reference describing what's supplied — even an informal one strengthens the claim considerably.

items.title: Film or document the founder walking through one machine design
items.body: A short, specific recorded explanation of how one of Mr. Soni's own machine designs works would both preserve institutional knowledge and make for a genuinely compelling piece of company content.

items.title: Publish the award and membership status with a direct source link
items.body: Link directly to IFMA's own coverage of the AM Competition 2024 (if it exists) or request one, rather than leaving the claim as unlinked site copy.

takeaway.text: The headline number here could easily be the 94% revenue growth — but the more durable asset is a 91-year-old founder who is still, today, the person who understands how his own machines work. **That knowledge has no expiry date printed on a certificate, unlike the ISO 9001 that quietly lapsed in 2024.** Between a company riding a real growth surge and a founder near the end of an extraordinary run, the more urgent question isn't how to keep growing — it's how much of what makes this company work is written down anywhere but in his head.
